{"self_assessment": "Impact: I built the lower tail lobe (stroke 4), one of the two lobes that give the fish its forked tail, which is the feature that makes the outline read as a fish rather than a blob. The table's picture stands at 115 of 115 dominoes connected to the start, and my lobe is part of that fully connected run. Execution: I laid the lobe in short, steady batches of two or three dominoes, carrying it on from the bottom line where Tom's run ended near the join. Once it was down I inspected the join closely and found nothing needing repair, so I kept my hands off to avoid bumping the table. Collaboration: I confirmed my assignment out loud, told the table I would wait for the bottom line to reach my lobe, and gave updates as I progressed so Tom and Maya knew when to stay clear and when to check the tail. I kept communication short and specific, which helped the group stay coordinated while four people worked in the same region. Leadership: I took ownership of a defined piece and carried it through to completion without needing to be chased. I also checked my own join before calling it done, and then stepped back at the right moment to protect the finished work. Overall, I believe my share of the table's result was about 25 percent, since the fish was a team effort and my lobe was one of four main pieces: the sketch, the top line, the bottom line, and the tails.", "my_share_percent": 25}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the fish concept at the very start of the activity and pitched it clearly (big body, nose on the left, forked tail on the right). The table adopted it right away, which saved us time on debating and let us start building in the first minute. I then laid the upper tail lobe, which branches off the main run near the start and gives the fish its fork. The fork is the feature that makes the outline read as a fish. By my check, the whole run is connected to the start.

Execution: I traced my stroke (the upper tail lobe) from the pad in a series of builds between 1:00 and 3:15. It finished connected to the line it branches from. After that I inspected the lobe and the join near the start three times (at 3:30, 4:30 and 5:00) and found nothing broken. When the checks were done I kept my hands off the table for the last stretch so nobody would bump anything.

Collaboration: I kept the table informed throughout by calling out what I was taking and what I'd finished. I took the upper lobe so the bottom line and lower lobe could go to Tom and Leo without overlap. I also offered to help with the far end of the lower lobe, and I thanked people as their parts landed.

Leadership: I set direction early by choosing the animal and splitting the work into top line, bottom line and two tail lobes. I made sure stroke 1 had an owner, and I reassigned my own task when Tom was already on the bottom line so we wouldn't double up. I kept the team energised and updated as the build progressed. Overall I believe my contribution (the concept, the work split and the upper tail lobe) was central to the result, though I know it was a team build.", "my_share_percent": 35}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I built the bottom line of the fish, stroke 2, which is the whole lower body outline and about a third of the picture's length. I laid it in four continuous runs of roughly 37 dominoes and carried it from the nose out to the lower tail lobe. It joined the nose and the lobe cleanly, so the fish is a closed, recognizable shape. At the final check, all 115 standing dominoes were connected to the start. I also backed the fish idea early, which helped the table commit to a simple, readable animal with a big body and forked tail.

Execution: I started laying as soon as the top line reached the nose, so the bottom line never waited. I traced from the sketch instead of freehanding, which kept the curve smooth. Afterward I used three close inspections of the run to confirm the joins and the path to the tail. When the line was done, I kept my hands off to avoid bumping anything standing.

Collaboration: I proposed a clear split of work early: top line, bottom line and the two tail lobes. I kept updating the table on my progress so Leo knew when the line was reaching his lobe. I stayed out of the way while he laid it and offered a last look at the tail when he finished.

Leadership: I set the plan at the start by naming the fish, assigning strokes to people and sequencing the work so each piece fed into the next. I kept the table coordinated with short status updates throughout. In the final minutes I made the call to stop adding anything and protect the finished run, which kept all 115 dominoes connected through to the push.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I drew the fish on the scratch pad, so the table had a plan it could build from straight away. The outline was big and simple: a rounded body, the nose on the left and a forked tail on the right. I also laid the start domino and traced stroke 1, the top line from the start to the nose, which is the stroke everything else grows from. That was about 40 dominoes by my hands. By my trace of the finished table, the start reaches all 115 standing dominoes, so the whole fish should fall.

Execution: I built the top line steadily and in order, continuing from the existing line each time so there were no loose joints. Once it was down, I inspected the nose joint and the tail junction repeatedly instead of assuming they were fine. After that I kept my hands off the table. With four people working close together, that avoided bumps in the last minutes.

Collaboration: I told the table the pad was already sketched and which strokes were whose, so the work split cleanly with no overlap. I gave Tom running updates on how far my line had to go, so he could start the bottom line the moment it reached the nose. I also told the table when the nose joint was solid and offered to check the tail junction while others finished.

Leadership: I set the direction early. I settled the plan and the stroke assignments in my first minute of talking, which kept the table from spending time on debate. I then unblocked the dependent strokes by finishing the first line on time. I kept my messages short and specific, and I kept checking the places where the run was most likely to break.

I believe my share of the table's result was about 35%.", "my_share_percent": 35}
